parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Queen's Knight Variation
parent.overview: The QGD with 3.Nc3 develops the knight and adds pressure on d5. The usual continuation is 3...Nf6, after which White chooses 4.Bg5 (pin; Black replies Orthodox 4...Be7, Cambridge Springs, Tartakower ...b6 or Lasker ...Ne4), 4.Nf3 or the Exchange 4.cxd5. Black holds d5 with ...e6, which gives a bulletproof centre but locks the c8 bishop; Black frees the game with ...c5 or ...e5, or ...b6 and ...Bb7. White's main plans are the minority attack (b4-b5 against c6) in Exchange structures, or central play with e4. Play is slow and technical rather than tactical, with a strong reputation for soundness, and the Cambridge Springs is the one trappy tactical sub-line.

parent.name: Hungarian Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.g3 to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2 and hit the long diagonal, deferring any central commitment (s1, s3). It is a flank opening that usually transposes: into the King's Indian Attack (Nf3, d3, O-O, then e4), the Catalan, the Réti or the English, depending on Black's set-up (s1, s3, s4). Black can happily occupy the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, or choose Sicilian, Caro-Kann or King's Indian-style set-ups (s2, s3). Positions are usually closed or flexible, with long-term strategic play rather than early tactics (s1, s3). Engines and statistics find it essentially equal, with White at most slightly more comfortable (s3, s4). Theory is minimal: it is closer to a move order than a distinct variation (s2).

parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.

parent.name: French Defense: Knight Variation
parent.overview: 2.Nf3 is a waiting move that leaves White's central structure undecided. After 2...d5 White can transpose to the Advance (3.e5 c5 4.d4, the subtree's main line), the Exchange (3.exd5 exd5 4.d4), main French lines (3.Nc3) or play for a King's Indian Attack set-up with d3, g3, Bg2 and castling. In the KIA the e5 square is held by pieces (Nf3, Re1) rather than the d4 pawn, which sidesteps the French d4 target. Black's replies are 2...d5 (by far the most common) and the rare 2...f5 (Franco-Hiva Gambit). It is treated in the sources as a secondary option rather than a main-line weapon, and the sources give little independent material on it.

parent.name: Englund Gambit
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...e5, offering the e-pawn after 2.dxe5 to avoid closed queen's-pawn positions and set tactical problems. The main line is 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3, where Black regains the pawn on b2 but loses the queenside attack; the gambit relies on traps such as 6.Bc3?? Bb4! with mate threats on c1. White can simply keep the pawn and, with accurate development, retains an advantage. Strong players and engines consider it unsound for Black, and top-level players almost never choose it. It scores through quick development and traps against an unprepared opponent.

parent.name: Old Indian Defense
parent.overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Alekhine Defense
parent.overview: Black attacks e4 at once with 1...Nf6 and, after 2.e5 Nd5, invites White to build a broad centre with c4, d4 and perhaps f4, planning to attack that centre later with ...d6, ...Nb6, ...Bg4, ...c5 and ...dxe5. White's job is to keep or use the extra space, either with the most ambitious Four Pawns Attack (4.c4 Nb6 5.f4), the popular Modern Variation 4.Nf3, or the less forcing Exchange 5.exd6; 2.Nc3 avoids the main line entirely. Positions lose symmetry from the start and are unbalanced, with a space edge for White against Black's counterplay on the overextended pawns. The opening is regarded as sound, original and tricky but risky (moderate to high), and is only moderately common at the top: Fischer, Korchnoi, Ivanchuk and occasionally Carlsen have played it.
